utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Before the witness will be brought in, I would like to raise one matter. On the 7th of July, the Chamber issued the so-called 92 bis decision and we have heard that the Prosecution had some problems with a list of witnesses and to categorise them. Last week on the 28th of September, the Chamber sent an e-mail it to the parties with some guidance how to arrange that. We would like to get an update during today's hearing, not at the moment. Perhaps you can provide us with the status of your compliance with this 7th July decision. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President, and everyone. Your Honours. Yes, Ms. Stewart tells me that we'll be uploading many of the witnesses by next week or if not all. All 92 bis with cross will be uploaded next week in e-court. And I will talk to Mr. Thayer about any other details or issues related to that and get updated. He has been sick so I haven't been able to talk to him, but I don't know if he's in today or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this update. That is appreciated. The Chamber was told that there is another procedural matter the Prosecution wants to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Last night when we accelerated to the two witnesses today, I realised that the Prosecution needed to ask you to give the warnings, the 90(E) warning, so I sent an e-mail to the Court Officer and to Mr. Gajic last night. I don't know if you got that. But as you'll recall, the 90(E) is where there may be some indication a witness is involved or close to the events, and what we are asking is that you let both of them know that they have a right under 90(E) to object to making statements which might incriminate them, but that if they do object, the Court may compel them to answer the questions, but -- and in that event, those compelled statements cannot be used against them. I think it's been awhile since we've done that, but that I wanted to ask you if you could do. You will see that -- and you know from the record that these witnesses were very closely involved in these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this recommendation. Indeed, one of the witnesses was told accordingly in the Popovic case, as I saw it in the transcript, and we -- I think we should proceed in that way. Are there any other matters to raise? This is not the case, then the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation to tell truth on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. The Court Officer will assist you. Are the earphones now situated in a proper manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is not the first time that you will testify in this Tribunal. You've done it earlier, and you will perhaps recall that the presiding judge in the Popovic case gave you some guidance and I would like to do the same. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we have a Rule 90 with a paragraph (E), and I would like to read it for your information. It is said in this paragraph: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." I think you were already told about these regulations. We were told that you were present at some stages in the events we are dealing with here in the Tribunal, so that you should be aware of your right to reject answers to some questions if this answer could incriminate yourself. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Prosecution has some questions for you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you first tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Ostoja Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall testifying in the Popovic case back in 16 and 17th of May, 2007?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you had a chance in the last two days to listen to your complete testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today or in the next days here, would your answers be the same as they were in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, I would like to offer P1074 into evidence. That is the transcript of the witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can note for the record that the associated exhibits admitted through this witness I would like to also offer. They should be on the sheet, but I can go over them briefly as P1075 through P1079, and then P00011, P1080, P1081, P1082, P1083 through P1087. Those are all the exhibits that I would offer that came in through this witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: All these documents will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now I'll read the summary. Mr. Stanisic was born in December 1951 in Fojnica. He served his compulsory military service with the JNA between 1977 and 1978 in the infantry branch of the school for reserve officers. Upon completion of his training, he was given the rank of sergeant. After his compulsory military service, he returned to Fojnica where he remained part of the reserved armed forces in the position of the security organ. In May 1992, he was mobilised into the armed forces of Republika Srpska as a captain. Mr. Stanisic remained in the Republika Srpska armed forces or VRS through 1995. In July 1995, Mr. Stanisic was the commander of the 6th Infantry Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, known as the Petkovci Battalion, which was headquartered in the village of Petkovci. On the morning of 14 July, 1995, Mr. Stanisic was at the battalion forward command post when he received two calls over the radio from the Zvornik Brigade deputy commander and Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic. Obrenovic ordered Stanisic to send 40 of his men to the Zvornik Brigade command to join the units that had been deployed in Snagovo. Mr. Stanisic reported to the Zvornik Brigade headquarters at the Standard Barracks with those men sometime before noon that day. He then returned to the forward command post around 1300, 1400 hours where he had a briefing with his company commanders. He returned to the battalion command post at the old school in Petkovci at around 1700 or 1800 hours that afternoon. When Mr. Stanisic returned to the battalion command post in Petkovci, his deputy, Marko Milosevic, told him that the Zvornik Brigade duty officer, Dragan Jokic, had radioed from brigade command to say that captured Muslim prisoners were supposed to arrive at the new school in Petkovci to be exchanged. By the time Stanisic had returned to the battalion command post, the prisoners had already arrived at the new school in Petkovci. Jokic called again and spoke to Stanisic directly. He asked Stanisic to find Colonel Beara, who was supposed to have been located somewhere around the new school in Petkovci. Stanisic testified that the duty officer told him that "Colonel Beara was supposed to be notified that he should report to the command." Stanisic asked, "Where, what command?" And the duty officer said, "Well, he knows well which command he's suppose today report to." Stanisic went to -- sent, excuse me, Stanisic sent Milosevic to find Colonel Beara. About half an hour later, Milosevic returned and reported back to Stanisic that he had found Beara with Zvornik Brigade assistant commander for security, Drago Nikolic, near the new Petkovci school. Milosevic informed Beara that he should report to his command. Milosevic also reported having seen buses and trucks at the school as well as some military police and soldiers. Stanisic notified the person on duty in the brigade command that Beara had received the message. During the afternoon -- and this is the 15 July -- excuse me, during the afternoon of the 14 July, Stanisic heard isolated shots or bursts of fire coming from the school. That night he stayed at the battalion command post at the old Petkovci school. He heard short bursts of fire into the night. The next morning, Stanisic was at the forward command post of the battalion where he received a call that villagers from Petkovci had come to his command complaining about the visibility and stench of corpses and requested a truck to remove the bodies near the new school and to clean the area. Stanisic released a truck to remove bodies and to clean the school on the morning of 15 July. Stanisic saw Zvornik Brigade deputy commander Dragan Obrenovic on the morning of 16 July on the left wing of the battalion's defence line. Stanisic stated that he told Obrenovic that he was angry at having to provide a lorry from the battalion for the civilians to remove the bodies and clean the school. Stanisic denied any knowledge that hundreds of prisoners were transported from the new school at Petkovci to the dam near Petkovci on the night of 15 July. He also denied any knowledge that large numbers of prisoners were buried at the dam near Petkovci during the day on 15 July. If I could ask a few questions to highlight some of those points. Could we bring up P1083.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as that's coming up, Mr. Stanisic, could you tell us at the time did you know the position of Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you know which division, whether it be brigade, corps, or Main Staff or some other that he was the security organ from?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Security organ attached to the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we have heard from your testimony that your deputy Marko Milosevic reported back to you that he did make this report to Colonel Beara and he saw Drago Nikolic with him. Can you tell us who Drago Nikolic was at the time on 14 July?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic was the security organ in the brigade. He was the chief of security in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at this document P1083, and is that your handwriting in blue on it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember creating this exhibit in court in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is -- generally what area is shown in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The village Petkovci and marked with a red circle and number 2 is the new school. Marked with number 1 is the old school where the battalion command was and houses which were inhabited are encircled with a blue pen. And it is indicated where the dam should be, the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us roughly how many kilometres the dam, the plateau of the dam is from the -- well, the new school at Petkovci? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Perhaps up to 2 kilometres or between 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly how long would it take to drive a truck from this little village of Petkovci over to that plateau of the dam?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, around 5 to 10 minutes. It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us again roughly where the front line was for your particular battalion? I mean, roughly how many kilometres up in those hills was it from the village of Petkovci?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The right wing of the defence was perhaps a kilometre away from the village, and the left wing was further away, maybe up to 2 or 3 kilometres because it stretched along a hill. It was 2 or 3 kilometres away from Petkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in those days when the Muslims from Srebrenica came through the Zvornik Brigade lines and there was fighting, roughly 14, 15, 16 July, did your battalion pick up any Muslim corpses and -- from the combat and do anything with them?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As for my defence sector, that is the defence sector of the 6th Battalion, we did not have any wounded Muslims or any Muslims who were killed. We were fighting at a distance from the direction of Nezuk, that was the 2nd Corps from Tuzla, and from the direction of Motovska Kosa, that was in depth in our territory and there were only -- there was only fire in the direction of Muslims, that is to say the column, until the moment when a truce was signed. We were firing with all the weapons and equipment that we had because I had to defend the front line. But we did not have any direct contact with the Muslim manpower and in this area, no Muslims were killed or taken prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what Zvornik battalion bore the brunt of that Muslim column where they actually had to deal with them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did you receive the interpretation of the last question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know, what Zvornik Brigade battalion had to do the most fighting with the Muslim column as it came from their rear?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It appears that there is a problem with the interpretation. I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, did you receive proper translation of the last portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I stop hearing the sound occasionally and I can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we should change the earphones and use another set. Sir, do you receive proper interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us which Zvornik Brigade battalion had to deal with the Muslim column as it approached from the rear? If you folks didn't have to deal with them so much, which battalion did, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The adjacent battalion to the left wing from me, that was the 4th Battalion, and the Muslim forces had practically passed through the line held by the 4th Battalion and attacked the command as well. Some soldiers got killed and were wounded on our side or were burned, and they managed to make a break-through across and through the line that was held by the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "they managed to break through," you are talking about who?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: About the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll be talking to the commander of the 4th Battalion soon enough. Sir, we've heard from your prior testimony that villagers -- you have said that villagers complained to you about corpses. Where were those corpses that they complained about?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The bodies were near houses and near the school building. There was population inhabiting the area nearby and it was in that area that they found the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've talked about two schools, the old school and the new school. Which school or perhaps both or where were the bodies found?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The new school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly how many bodies, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know the exact number, was it two or three corpses, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if -- how do you explain their deaths if there were -- you did not retrieve any battle casualties from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, probably since they had been transported there and placed there, they must have been killed by those who brought them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who brought them there, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: According to what I learned from my deputy Mr. Milosevic who had told me that he had informed Colonel Beara, he saw trucks and buses there, and he saw soldiers with white belts, presumably since it was the military police who normally had these white belts, one could assume that they were members of the military police. Which unit is something that we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as you've told us, Mr. Milosevic told Beara to report. Did Colonel Beara come by your battalion headquarters to make any communications to report to anyone that day or any other day?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Nobody came to the battalion command. Nobody came to the command on that day, and later on I was up at the combat positions and I had no way of knowing if anybody had come to the command or not. It was practically abandoned, in other words. There was only the logistics platoon present there, as well as the guards. My entire command personnel, as well as some of the auxiliary personnel were up on the defence line manning these positions. I had to compensate for the 40 men that I lost because I had to send them to Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic, the chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that this message that Colonel Beara was coming -- came from the brigade duty officer. Where was the brigade duty officer calling from when he made this report to you and Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The brigade duty officer was supposed to be at the brigade command within the Standard facility in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And had Colonel Beara gone back to that brigade command from Petkovci, roughly how long would it have taken him to drive from Petkovci to the Standard Barracks in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately 20 minutes. Between 10 and 20 minutes. It all depends on the speed at which you drive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It was a hard asphalt road the entire way, or was there gravel?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The entire road was asphalted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And once present at the Zvornik Brigade, would he have had the ability or would anyone have had the ability to communicate from the Zvornik Brigade headquarters to the headquarters of the Main Staff at Crni Rijeka or Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to P1085. There should be an English version and a B/C/S version and we need to flip it around so we can read it. And I think the -- it needs -- that's it. And if we could focus, well, first on the first page so we can see the number of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a TAM 75.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, we need to get the complete document because I need the vehicle number which is just off to the right. Sorry, you can keep that page up on the B/C/S, but we need the page on the right on the English -- there we go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can now see that this is registration number M-5329. What is a TAM 75?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for switching it. We did now need to switch to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But can you tell us what a TAM 75 is?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It's a lorry with the carrying capacity of 2.5 tonnes and it has a -- it's covered in tarp with a wooden frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if there are -- are there sometimes benches in the back that soldiers can sit in?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. We normally use these vehicles to transport troops to positions. There were inhabited settlements nearby and they were soldiers. I could use these vehicles to transport my men in an emergency or for regular shifts of soldiers, depending on the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many soldiers could you really push together in the back of a TAM 75 if you needed to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: With weapons and full gear, perhaps 15 to 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page in both English and B/C/S, if we could. And let's first blow up the handwritten B/C/S. We are looking for 15 July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can't see the date properly. It should be moved a little bit to the right. The other way around, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think that's pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm looking for that first entry on 15 July, it says "Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci." Now, when it says "Brana" what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Brana is the dam, the only one that was there with the red sludge, and it's the aluminium and you have the alkaline waste there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was this TAM 75 doing going to the dam that day from the village of Petkovci and back again?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, probably since the villagers were looking to obtain a lorry given that there were corpses there, they drove them over to where that red sludge was. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That's what they said, that they were corpses, so they -- I mean, transported the corpses to the dam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened to the corpses at the dam, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Believe me when I say that I don't know what happened next. I wasn't there. I only returned to brigade command -- or rather the battalion command on the 16th or the 17th when the line was reformed, when the situation calmed down, and once the Muslims had already gone out of the Srebrenica area through the open corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's move this over from right to left so that we get the right side of both things so we can see more information on this sheet. Okay. Right there. That's good. Now -- right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see here that under one of the boxes it's "journeys" and "people," and if we look at this particular entry, Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci, I think if we could get your help and start over to the left and just slowly move to the right so we can try to keep track of where it is. So if we start at Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci and just slowly go over, and we'll see that -- okay, right there we have four journeys and 1 plus 8 people. So if there's four journeys back and forth to Petkovci, is that what that means?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when it says 1 plus 8 people, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It should stand for driver plus the number of passengers driven. In this case, one would be the driver and eight would be the number of passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So those four trips with eight people, that's 32 passengers. Who were those 32 passengers?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Here, well this -- believe me when I tell you that it's inexplicable. Four would be shifts or trips, so would you perhaps have eight men in each of the shifts or the trips, or was it a different arrangement. I don't think that anyone can explain this other than the person who wrote it. Well, look here below, you have 1 plus 6, so that would mean one trip where six people were taken somewhere, but as for this other number, I don't think I can clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we know Parlog, that was probably the front line and that was probably taking soldiers to the front line to help the fighting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: That's possible too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The dam was just a few kilometres from your headquarters, was there any fighting going on at the dam on the 14th and 15th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No. There was no fighting. The soldiers from my battalion had no purpose there because they had no orders that would take them there. I told you already that all the personnel that I had at my disposal, even those who were resting at the time, were called up by me and were deployed to the positions. Next to the dam you have the village of Djulici where men from Bircani were stationed who were also members of my unit so 1 plus 8, I don't know what it means. They would also be taken to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to one more document, it's P1090.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, Judge Mindua want to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my apologies, Mr. Prosecutor. Witness, I'm still dealing with the same document, P1085. And I'm still dealing with the same entry. We have talked about the figure 1 and 8, but on the left-hand side, I see "out of service." What exactly was out of service? I'm just wondering. Could this be the actual meter or was it the vehicle itself? What was out of service? The Prosecutor might help you in answering the question, but then we have the figure 35, this has not been explained either, so there are two questions, the figure 35 and the mention of out of service. This will help us to better understand this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it. Oh, yes, "starting at," this meant that the counter of the number of kilometres travelled was out of service or wasn't working properly and that would tell you the number of kilometres travelled. In other words, the driver was unable to establish by looking at the counter what the status of kilometres travelled was. Rather, he had to write down an estimate of the kilometres travelled and we needed this to have proper records kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as for figure 35 on the right-hand side, it is actually linked to what it says next to it, namely "out of service," it's because the odometer wasn't working and therefore the driver felt that they had driven 35 kilometres in this instance, is that what you are saying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I understand better now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The document that we have on the left-hand side, which is the original, is not consistent with or does not correspond to the one on the right-hand side because it states that the metre -- the kilometre count was out of order and yet we have the number of kilometres stated there. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I would like to invite you to dwell on that a little bit further to understand fully this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know what he is talking about. They are the same and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. There's indeed a problem. We see on the right-hand side kilometre counter starting at 350.193 kilometres and this is at least illegible on the left-hand side, the original B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll look into that, that's a translation error. I don't understand that. That's a good point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems, if that is true, it seems to be a very old car, but it could be understandable that the kilometre counter is not moving, but this is all speculation. Do you have any idea, witness, about this kilometre number on the left-hand side? We can't see something, only "kilometre" but perhaps Mr. McCloskey has the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll get the original document, but I'm confident that that is a decent scan of it. There are many, many of these documents, they come in a big stack and the translators may have interspersed one for the other and we'll get to the bottom of that. That's a good point and we'll try to find out where that is coming from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the column number 9, Judge Mindua was putting a question to that. For me it's not clear yet. In the headline in the translation it is said "archived TKM/PKM expression unknown." It is column number 9. Sorry, I misread. It is "achieved," not "archived." That was my mistake. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stanisic, if you could help us with that column number 9. We see a sideways Cyrillic writing, can you read that for us in your language and tell us what it means, if you know?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I know little of such logs. What I do know is that all these numbers that we have there, 30, 50, and so on, that they stand for the amount of kilometres travelled on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I understand that, but can you read out the word, I'm sure you can read the word that's at the top of number 9 and the initials there?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: "Achieved TKM/PKM." Well, TKM, I don't know what it stands for. And PKM might be -- no, I don't know, really. I can't clarify this for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to the first page of the document in both languages. If we go to the right side of each document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the first page in B/C/S as well. It's coming up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see here that they are -- someone is accounting -- looks like they are accounting for fuel in this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't realise it was addressed to me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, tell the Chamber how important a commodity fuel was at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, fuel was very important. Practically as much as gold. There were shortages everywhere so it was highly valued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how important was keeping track of the fuel and the kilometres used in relation to that fuel?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As we were supplied by the brigade, they approximately knew or actually they knew the kilometres and judging by these vehicle logs, they would approve the amount of fuel, judging by the number of kilometres. That was how they decided how much fuel to approve for our use. There may have been just 5 or 6 litres of fuel in a vehicle, just so that it could reach Standard, and if it needed to go anywhere further from Standard then it would be filled up with fuel in accordance with the number of kilometres as stated on the vehicle log. It depended on what the destination was. If the distance was greater, there would be more fuel assigned. If it was shorter, then it would be less fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 1090.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is another vehicle log. And our last log P1085 was for vehicle M-5329 and we should see -- if we could go to the first page, that this is M-5300. And this is a TAM 80. Can you tell us what the difference is between a TAM 75 which was the last vehicle and a TAM 80 which is this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, both vehicles were almost identical. Perhaps TAM 80 was a later model. It also had one plus two cab and it also had the bed which was like a box with tarpaulin. There weren't any great differences between the two. Its capacity was also up to 2.5 tonnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at this one a bit like we did the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's go to the next page in both languages. In the B/C/S let's -- I think there should be a page before this one. There you go. And could we -- let's blow this up. And let's go to this -- the section that the General pointed out that was a problem on the other one. Can we go to -- all right, let's -- we'll start right where this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And again I want us to look at 15 July, and I think we can see it down there. Again it says "Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci." And this one has 0900 to 1100 hours. And let's go slowly to the right so we can see what else it says. Okay let's stop there. We do see a word this time in section 5 and it says "starting at." And then I think it's handwritten "not working." Is that correct in section 5?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see in the first line it says again "not working," and then we see the little hash-marks that go all the way down it. Do those little hash-marks mean not working all the way down for each of these days?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes. The odometer in the vehicle was not working, device that counts the number of kilometres travelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this truck's was broken as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's slowly go across at Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci, left to the right, please. We see six journeys. Okay, that's fine. Okay. And stop right there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see this time 1 plus 5 and then for kilometres 48. So is your explanation for this any different than the last one; 1 is the driver, 5 is the passengers?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this one is 6 -- 6 journeys, unlike the last one that was 4, and so we have a total of 48 kilometres, which is a few more than the last one. So is that -- does that reflect your understanding of this document like the last one?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that would mean that there's 30 people taken to the dam in six journeys on the morning of the 15th of July. Let me just ask you, do you know if those people were in the back were alive or dead?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, I don't know. I cannot interpret whether five men were transported during each of the trips, but I would go back to the 15th of July here where it says Petkovci-Srebrenica. Can we just move the document a little bit so as to show that. A little bit more, please. The 15th of July, so it's one in the same date. Here we can see the 15th of July and that the vehicle left for Srebrenica on the 15th of July at 8.00 in the morning and returned at 1000 hours. And then on the same day it also took the trip Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci. During my previous testimony, I also said that this is impossible because I know that this vehicle left for Srebrenica at 8.00 in the morning on the 15th. It left for Srebrenica and returned on the 16th. So it spent the night in Srebrenica and only returned on the following day, so this vehicle log is not clear to me at all. And these trips recorded here, it is impossible that a vehicle should go from Petkovci to Srebrenica and return in two hours because this is an old vehicle, a TAM, which can go perhaps up to 60 or 70 kilometres per hour and not any faster. There were already combat activities going on along this axis so that some barricades were put up, the military police controlled the road, and what I learned from the driver, the vehicle returned via Serbia because it couldn't return along the same route which it took from Srebrenica to Zvornik because the Muslim forces were already on some sections of the road and it was not safe to drive. This is why I find this vehicle log completely illogical. For a vehicle to go from 8.00 to 10.00 to Srebrenica and then on the same day from 10.00 and later in two hours that it should drive there and return, you couldn't do that even in peacetime and if you had a good vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, perhaps you have an explanation for my following observation. On the 15th of July, you were discussing the entry Petkovci-Srebrenica. There's no mention of returning back to Petkovci. The next entry it is Petkovci-Brana-Petkovci and if you compare that with the other entries, there's always return to Petkovci, not with this entry you were referring to. Do you have an explanation for that? Perhaps it was a one-way trip without a return at that day or what could be the explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know the vehicle left for Petkovci and then from Petkovci to Srebrenica. It returned on the following day. Now, why the driver did not write down the return, I don't know. Only the driver could be asked this question or whoever was driving this vehicle. Why what is recorded is just the one-way trip. But I'm 100 per cent sure that the vehicle left at 8.00 in the morning and that it returned on the following day, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because I approved for this vehicle to leave. It was a soldier of mine, a platoon commander who was killed in Srebrenica because he was sent there with the tactical group. I sent 20 soldiers there and he was their commander and he was killed and he could not be found immediately. At the insistence of his brother, I approved for the vehicle with a few soldiers to go there and try to look for him. They didn't find them then but only several days later. This is why I know that the vehicle left for Srebrenica because it had to do with a soldier who had disappeared, it was this commander of a platoon, a commander who was leading 20 men with the tactical group which participated in combat around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might give you the original. You can see -- it may help in your questioning or my questioning, there's different colour ink on these days in different handwriting Cyrillic versus Latin. And so if you want to get into those details, I have this which I think you may be interested in seeing. It's the original for this, the one that he is talking about. And if the witness could see it too, it may help him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see the original. That would be helpful, yes. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Witness, perhaps you may help me understand things better. On the document we see that there are Cyrillic writings. Could we look on the right-hand side of the document. Could we move it a bit more, there we go. A bit more. There we go, thank you. Witness, the last column of this document is dealing with the kilometres, and I would like you to read out what it says on top so that we have a translation. What does it say above this column so that we have a translation in our respective languages? What is the heading just above column number 10, there are three lines, three headings. Could you please tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kilometres, party position. Is this what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please move it a little bit further in both languages. Go ahead. Please continue moving. Yes, thank you. And in B/C/S as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that it tallies more or less. Thank you very much. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I could ask him about the various -- to examine that, the various handwritings, the inks and all, we might as well ask him, maybe he will be able to help us, maybe not, but it should probably be on the ELMO so we can see what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stanisic, if you could go to that area you pointed out, the trip to Srebrenica, and the trip to Brana where there is that one hour time glitch that you've pointed out, and you'll note --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we are going to have to blow it up a bit and let's get to the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can -- if we look at the two entries on the 15th, the one that's in Cyrillic, it says Petkovci-Srebrenica, and the one below that is in Latin, and I imagine if we go over and see the signature on the end of it, there may be -- it's going to be hard to tell exactly who is who in looking at it like this, but how would you explain that one person is -- one is writing in Cyrillic and one is Latin, and you can look at the whole document. Can you make out the signatures?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Here is my signature, Stanisic it says. And below that, whether it's Milan, Milan ... it could be a Milan but I can't see here. One of the signatures is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you look at the original document. The Court Officer will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there it is. Stanisic. And this other one seems to be Milan. Milan something. Or Milutin. It could be Milutin as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just to clear it up, Stanisic has been signed for the trip to Srebrenica that's 130 kilometres, which would reflect, that's back and forth to Srebrenica, isn't it, 130?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's a mistake, Mr. McCloskey. This is the one line above. Stanisic is at the line 64 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's the Srebrenica one that I'm curious about because the Srebrenica one is the same one for the dam and so it's those two in red. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The two in red is where I wanted you to look. The 130 and 48, whose signature is that? Is it different or the same?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Believe me I'm not a handwriting expert, but in my view they are similar. It seems to be someone Milan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you've told us how important fuel is and we see the commander's signature on this, so I'm sure it was someone important, wasn't it? Can you tell us who that was that signed it?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It's possible that the assistant commander for logistics signed it because he was keeping the records in terms of logistics. Milan Stanisic. And there was also -- he was also -- there was also a commander of the logistics platoon, Milan Peric, and also a technical service clerk and traffic service clerk, Milutin. So any of these three could have signed these travel orders. Milan Stanisic, Milan Eric who unfortunately got killed after the war, and Milutin Acimovic. So these are three persons. And I signed in the absence of the assistant commander for logistics, my assistant, I signed the travel order so that the vehicle could go to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last thing, let's go to the other end of the document and look at the original because we can see in those two entries, the Srebrenica in Cyrillic entry and the Brana entry, that -- go all the way to the other end, please. There we go. We can see that there's different colours -- different coloured ink from the dates that's written to the actual times. Do you have any explanation why it is that black ink would have been used for the date, 15-7, and then we see blue written in for the times?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't. I know that the drivers would enter something. Whether it was perhaps the driver who entered the time and the trip that was made and then the signature was -- it depends on the ball-point pen that they had. Not every driver had the same ball-point pen, he could have borrowed it from somebody else, or it hadn't been issued to him, it would depend which ball-point pen he would got hold of, then he would use it to sign this. Otherwise, I really don't have any other explanation as to why this would be in various colour. Probably depended on the pen they could get hold of. The one they had, they would sign with it and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it possible that -- when I was a truck driver, you were supposed to write in your time at the time it happened, but truck drivers don't always do that and they have to come back and fill it in correctly. So is it possible this is filled in after the original time by a truck driver that forgot or by somebody else to make the document tally so it could go to logistics without getting you in trouble?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Everything is possible. As for overseeing the records kept, I did not pay much attention to that as a commander. My assistant was in charge of it. The commander could not see to everything. As a commander, my role had to do with combat readiness and the rest. Others had to take care of their respective fields, assistant commander for logistics was one, assistant commander for morale was second, et cetera. They all had their own respective fields like security, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question. This Trial Chamber has heard that many of the Muslims at that school on these days were killed at the school and then their bodies transported to the dam and buried. They've also heard that hundreds of Muslims from that school were transported alive to the Brana, to the dam close by, and murdered. As the commander of that battalion, what, if anything, do you know about those -- that -- those facts?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As far as the transportation of the Muslims was concerned from the school building to the dam, I really don't know who transported them or when. I was manning the positions in the area of responsibility of my battalion at the forward command post. I took care to maintain the line and to maintain the adequate level of combat readiness, to have enough ammunition and men. That was my main preoccupation since at the time there was fighting going on, there were attacks against us. I was unable to know what was going on at the school because my lines were as many as 3 or 4 kilometres away from the school. It all depended on which wing of defence I attended to. My forward command post was located right in the middle of the defence line, so I really don't know who transported hundreds of people from the school to the red sludge dam and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we break, I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir or Mr. Gajic if you have had the opportunity to see the original log-book which was on the ELMO? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't had an opportunity so far, but we can do so over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that would be appreciated. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and we have the original for the other one as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: P1085. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to mention that the last -- the document on the ELMO now, that is P1090, is not tendered yet by the Prosecution. It was not on the list you mentioned this morning, and I would like to mention that the documents P1077 and 1078 have no translation yet, therefore those will be only marked for identification pending translation. And I would like to point out that the document P00011 was not admitted through this witness, Stanisic in the Popovic case, but through witness Ljubo Bojanovic on the 29th of November, 2009. I leave it for the moment like it is and we must have our first break now. The Court Officer will assist you during the break. We adjourn and resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime during the break, we got a request for moving the tomorrow sitting to the morning because there is an urgent need for a courtroom in the afternoon, there's no courtroom available for another Chamber. The Chamber agreed and we are very optimistic that the parties would agree to that as well. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was -- I am scheduled for a doctor's appointment tomorrow morning, but I'm sure you will welcome Mr. Vanderpuye in my place and I'm sure he will welcome the last-minute assignment, so we'll be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very nice formulation, he will welcome the last-minute assignment. Thank you very much for your understanding. Could you tell us something about the documents I mentioned -- sorry, I didn't see that. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Greetings to everyone and may this day in the court and the final judgement reflect God's will and not mine. I would like to say something on the change of schedule for tomorrow. I am not opposed to you proceeding as you deem fit, but I do oppose to it if it affects the preparation of the Defence. We need to spend 18 hours perhaps preparing witnesses, but if I have to spend all that time preparing, you will understand that I will only go back to my quarters at 8.00 in the evening and will have to be here again at 8.00 in the morning, so just when you make these changes please bear in mind these difficulties that the Defence has to contend with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think this is a very important point you made and we always try to be aware of that and to give you the chance to prepare properly. We are sitting today in the morning so that the afternoon would be free for your preparation. If that is too heavy burden, then you should say it and we have to try to make -- to find another arrangement, but you know we have only three courtrooms, at the moment only two courtroom, one courtroom is not working, and that is a big problem for all the Trial Chambers at the moment. We always try to acknowledge your position, but if you could agree for tomorrow's session, we would be very pleased.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I do agree to tomorrow's change of session. However, my legal assistant and I cannot be in contact after 8.00 in the evening. I can even perhaps give him a phone call, but he is unable to come and see me in the detention. The only thing I can do after those hours is sleep. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding and we will bear in mind your position for all future scheduling purposes. Mr. McCloskey, before the break I mentioned that you haven't tendered P1090 yet, and the Chamber would appreciate to have the original documents, P1090 and P1085, we have seen on the ELMO with a different colour of the entries. In e-court we have only black and white, so there was a discussion about the colour and therefore it would be appreciated if we could have that as well. What is your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've got a good scanner that we can scan in colour on this document and so that it will be clearer for you and then we'll bring those into e-court. That shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your request for leave is granted to change this document from black and white to the coloured version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clear up the other points you mentioned, P1090 which is what I was apparently using, is the same as the document that we entered into evidence P1084 with the addition of two more pages. Apparently the 20 -- right at the end of the month was not on the document that went into evidence, and so we just would -- I think we would offer 1090 into evidence so we have the complete document as well as the two pages that were useful. So I would offer 1090, the complete four-page version into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received with this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we also -- this P0011, Ms. Stewart checked that and confirmed that it actually came in through the Defence, 5DP00327 through this witness in the Popovic trial, so Ms. Stewart says we are correct in that regard so it should be in that section. Our records indicate that this witness's name is on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will check that if the record reflects that properly and we already made the decision to admit that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we turn to the Defence, Mr. Tolimir will examine you in cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May I again greet everyone present as well as the witness. And may this day in court and the final judgement reflect God's will. I do acknowledge what the Prosecutor stated to him in the beginning and the witness is free to indicate whenever he does not wish to answer any of my questions. I know that he took part in the fighting and that I cannot insist on matters that were defined as sensitive as such in his chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we speak the same language, we should both be mindful of the need to make a slight pause before speaking for the sake of interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now call up 11593, lines 23 through 25. And that's again page 11594, lines 2 and on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the Popovic case in response to the Prosecutor's question about your military career, you stated and I quote: "In the beginning I worked as a security organ for awhile for the 6th Battalion when the attack on Gladjansko Brdo started. From that moment on I was assistant battalion commander or in fact battalion commander." Can you tell us the date when the attack on Gladjansko Brdo started so that we may place it within a time-period?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the battalion was established early on in 1992 and it was the 6th Infantry Battalion. We are talking 1992. I was assigned to the battalion as a security organ. On the 6th of November, the battalion came under an attack from Muslim units led by Naser Oric. The area which the battalion defended was at Gladjansko Brdo. That was when we sustained casualties, we had quite a few people taken prisoner or gone missing. After the fall, the commander was removed and I was appointed the commander of the 6th Battalion which bore this title at the time. I suppose that you are confused by the title of the battalion, namely its number, number 6. Over time, there were constant transformations within the brigade and so at one point the 6th Battalion was renamed the 5th Battalion. At the time I had already been re-assigned to a new battalion that was established as a new 6th Battalion. For instance, what was formerly the 3rd Battalion was renamed the 2nd Battalion. This was the transformation that took place whereby the battalion names changed. So what was the 6th Battalion in 1992 was not the battalion that held the positions at the Sapna river and Baljkovica river later on. So that's why you might be confused by the fact that there is mention of these two different 6th Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was in November 1992 that you were assigned to the position of the battalion commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've mentioned the attack by the forces led by Naser Oric. Can you tell us if you took part in the fighting at the time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As a security organ or security officer, since quite a few individuals had abandoned their positions along the line, as I conducted the review, I requested for the manpower levels to be filled up. I was ordered by an officer, I can't remember who, to come to the Standard Barracks where I would be given two buses in order to collect the men who were assigned to that battalion in order to man it. However, in the morning hours of the 6th of November, an attack was launched on Gladjansko Brdo. Instead of setting out to gather these men, I had to go to the command post, but by that time the whole front line and the post had fallen. What I did instead was to participate in the pullout of the units that were under my command. In sum, that was the activity I took part in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you participated in the pullout of these units, as you've just told us, and in addressing the results of the attack thereafter, can you tell us what the losses were that your units sustained in that attack on Gladjansko Brdo?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: We withdrew to what were formerly our positions near Zvornik and the battalion was practically in disarray. Many of the companies lost its members through desertion, et cetera, and roughly 120 men were either killed or gone missing from the Zvornik Battalion. Out of my battalion, roughly 40 men were gone, six went missing and the rest were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The six individuals who went missing, were they subsequently found or were they later on listed as killed?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Out of the six missing, two were found but four are still considered missing, that's at least to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sustain any losses after the attack, that's to say when you've already lost your positions, or were these losses inflicted on your unit in combat?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: As far as those killed are concerned, there were those who were killed in combat and there were also those who were taken prisoner and subsequently executed. They were tied to tree trunks with wire, at least that's how we found them. By that time I was busy reforming the battalion and gathering all the survivors. We went out of the area of combat to do so. In various ditches and elsewhere people were found tied up to trees with barbed wire, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to ask you about that because that's something that you heard of, and I'll be asking these questions of those who were eye-witnesses. Tell us, were you appointed the battalion commander right away on the 6th?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: It was in the night between the 7th or the 8th, I don't know, that the brigade commander summoned me to the headquarters and told me that he would appoint me the battalion commander, in spite of the fact that I told him that there were active-duty officers there who would perhaps have been a better choice. He insisted that I should be the man and the appointment came two or three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I performed the duty of battalion commander for perhaps a month or a month and a half when a new commander was appointed, I believe it was Nikolic, I don't know his first name, and Major Strbac. They were my successors. That was when I was appointed battalion assistant commander and then when it came to this latter day 6th commander, that I became the battalion commander again once the actual battalion commander was wounded. So I was basically there to patch up all the holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We were able to see that it was during this one night that you stopped being the security officer and became a battalion commander. Did the brigade commander have the absolute right to appoint you to whatever position he saw fit, or did he need anyone's approval in that?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, believe me when I tell you that I don't know. He summoned me and told me that I was to be the battalion commander. Now, did he have to have somebody's approval, did he receive it? I don't know. I only know that he called me to him and informed me that as of such and such a date, I don't know which, I would be the commander of the 6th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters. After that, after this event on Gladjansko Brdo, were you ever sent back, once you were appointed as commander were you ever sent back to your duty in security organs?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: No, I was never returned to the duty of security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber whether the commander when holding meetings before you were relieved from your post, did he have the right to order you just like any other officer who was part of the commanding officers within the brigade? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I apologise, General, can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll repeat the question. Your brigade commander, could he issue orders to you just as he did to all the other commanding officers from the brigade command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, to me as a battalion commander he could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could he issue any order to you that had to do with battalion activities?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I may be wrong, but I thought the General was asking the witness if his commander could order him as a security officer to do things and I may be -- because that's the way it first was translated to me, and then it got turned into could his commander order him as the commander of the battalion, and it's two different things so I'm not sure which one the General meant and it may have been translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that, Mr. Tolimir. Perhaps you put the question again. But the answer was quite clear, I think. The answer was "yes, to me as a battalion commander he could." But.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But my point was I think he asked as a security officer could your commander order you, I think that was the question, and -- but that's what confused me because the answer was as a battalion commander my commander could order me. So that was my confusion on the issue because I thought it was the other way around, the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will ask the question again and let the witness answer and then we can draw the conclusions so that I wouldn't be doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As a member of your brigade, could your brigade commander issue orders to you just as he could to all other members, and I mean orders that had do with combat activities that the brigade was involved in?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that the answer is clear. Let us clarify anyway. Does that mean that the brigade commander is authorised to issue orders to all his subordinates who are within the composition of the brigade and who are lower than him in terms of rank and position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us be even more precise. Does the brigade commander have the right to issue orders to security organs so that it wouldn't be imputed -- we didn't ask everything, now I'm asking you this, so my question is whether the brigade commander has the right to issue orders to security organs? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, whatever the commander personally thinks that the security organ can do, that he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the brigade commander evaluate the work of all commanding officers in the brigade and also issues commandments and gives praise and so on?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your work monitored while you were brigade commander and while you were the security organ? Did command organs monitor your work and did they have the right to control it and monitor it in the sense of -- but you should answer the way you find fit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: When I was the battalion commander, the brigade commander had every possible authority to monitor me, control my work, request me to send all kinds of reports, so he had full control of me. As for the security organs, he could also do that in terms of relations within the brigade. He could exert some sort of monitoring over me and the security organs in the brigade. As you know, the security organs are commanded both horizontally and vertically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But this command only relates to the part of the duties which you discharge as part of the brigade command, as an officer during war time?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, only within the brigade, that is to say within my battalion. I was supposed to submit certain reports, combat reports, and so on. All the activities that I was carrying out should have been monitored by the commander through his subordinates, that is to say, through his assistants and the chiefs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The security organs who were superior to you within the brigade or outside the brigade, if there were such organs within the brigade, could they point out to you in the professional sense what was the work that you should do in the brigade and the manpower within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's important in that question to know if he is referring to Mr. Stanisic as a battalion commander or as the security officer. It was left general and we need to know whether or not it has to do with either of those two. You can't tell from the question and answer, but he has been talking about both, so it needs to be clear which one he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, you have heard what the Prosecutor has said, I will ask you the question and you should answer it. The superior security organ, I'm not sure at which level you had it, was it authorised to provide you with guide-lines as to how you should do some work that your brigade or battalion was charged with, and I mean in professional terms did they do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: I will put myself in the position of a security organ now, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: My superior specifically, that was Drago Nikolic, provided me with guide-lines and instructions as to what I should do and where the focus of my work should be within the battalion. At the same time, the battalion commander, I'm talking of myself as the security organ now, I was subordinated also to the battalion commander, and from him I could also receive orders and I did. For example, a certain number of soldiers had deserted from the front line so Stanisic please find the police, go to such and such villages, these are the addresses, go there with the police, take them into custody and so on. So that was my work as the security organ in the battalion. So, I apologise, but let me clarify what were the security organs in a battalion actually doing and what was I doing personally while I was the security organ, and of course if some tasks were issued to me or some guide-lines by the chief of security, whether there were any attempts at theft or anything, that was the kind of duties that I had to perform as a security organ in relation to the chief of security and the battalion commander. I believe that now I have answered and explained this as much as I know. I'm not an active-duty officer, so I'm not sure if I said everything, but I do know what I was doing. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Awhile ago you said that your superior along the line of security organs would provide you with guide-lines on how to perform a task such as return these soldiers to their unit, but who would issue the order that they should return to the units, the commander or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the security organ could provide with you guide-lines as to how to perform this task as best as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did the battalion commander have the authority to decide eventually how one of the tasks would be carried out, whether somebody would be taken into custody or released or not and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Well, the battalion commander on the basis of the list of company commanders who sent him these lists, how many people were missing from each company, the battalion commander would then call the security organ, provide him with a list, and say please take these men into custody. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are any questions by anyone else, we'll ask you these questions. I'm trying to ask the questions directly so that everyone would understand your role. Thank you. Now, please, while you had the role of battalion commander and were on the defence line against Nezuk. I will now focus on this group of questions because I think we have clarified your role while you were the security organ and were performing these task. That was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we are moving to the period of 1995 while you were performing the role as a battalion commander and were charged with defence tasks. As I said, I will not ask you about things that you said you didn't know during examination-in-chief. I will ask you what you do know and what you can answer, so if you can answer, just do so, please. Can you tell me what was the number of the battalion you were in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The 6th Infantry Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where this 6th Infantry Battalion of yours was located at the moment when the Muslims tried to break through from your rear and through your defence line in the direction of the Muslim forces which were facing your defence lines? Did you understand the question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: Yes, the defence sector of the 6th Battalion, to right it was the right bank of the Sapna river, Petrova Strana, and on the left 2 to 300 metres from the Baljkovica stream or river. In terms of depth, the village of Kitovnice and Grbovci village. That was in depth. And the command post was the old school in Petkovci and the forward command post on Petrova Strana.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to have a complete answer for those of us who are not soldiers, can you just please tell us whether, as you said, the defence sector of the 6th Battalion was the right bank of the Sapna river, and on the left?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The Baljkovica river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that the defence sector, just to clarify that? What is the difference between the zone of responsibility and the defence sector, just to make it clear for all the participants in this trial. Can you draw the distinction between the defence sector and the zone of responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The defence sector is something I'm not really familiar with. I know that the battalion has its sector, its the sector of defence, and the brigade has a zone, that is to say the zone of responsibility. So the brigade has a zone of responsibility and the battalion has a sector, whether the zone of responsibility and the sector are one in the same ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you now please explain what's the difference between these two, the defence sector and the zone of responsibility of a defence sector?

utterances.speaker: OSTOJA STANISIC
utterances.text: The defence sector is at the battalion level. The battalion defence -- can you hear me? A certain territory. And it's a small area. I have mentioned the kilometres, it's 2 to 3 kilometres wide and 3 to 5 kilometres deep. And the brigade's zone of responsibility is a wider area and it comprises, specifically in case of the Zvornik Brigade, it was adjacent to the Bijeljina Brigade on one side and on the Sekovici Brigade on the other. So it's a more general term. It includes the forward front line and also the depth of territory. It includes the free territory. That's as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to translate this into language that's clear to everyone who's not a soldier, does that include the spaces in between and the surfaces that cannot be -- that can be defended by fire, and that are in range and so on? Thank you.
